posed of spine-like divisions that radiate
in all directions, making diameter of eight

distribution these spherical heads, with
their elastic spines. are blown away by the
winds and roll swiftly away over the level
shore for miles, dropping seeds as they go.

their spines serve as sails, so that they can
cross estuaries. A plant valuable for taking
root in the sand and protecting the shores
from erosion, is thus widely distributed, as

birdless region.

Sherman was on the 4th Of July, in 1919,
In Independence Square. He was then
ninety-one and becoming very feeble,
but though old, his dimming eyes re-
kindled as he looked at Independence
Hall, which he said he had come to gaze
upon once more before he was gathered
home.

"What time is it?" said he, raising
his trembling hand. "What time is it?
I can see so well as I used to—"

"Past three."

"Come then," he continued, "let us go
into the hall. I want to tell you an inci-
dent in Washington's life no one
alive knows except myself, and if you live
long enough you will see it verified. Mark
me, I am not superstitious, but you will
see it verified."

Reaching the visitors rooms, in which
the sacred relics of our early days are
preserved, we sat down upon one of the
fashioned benches, and my venerated
friend related to me the following nar-
rative, which from the peculiarity of our
national affairs at the present time, I
have been induced to give to the world,
give it as nearly as possible in his own
words.

When the bold action of our Congress
in asserting the Independence of the col-
onies became known in the world, we were
laughed and scoffed at as silly, presumptu-
ous rebels, whom the British grenadiers
would tame to submission; but quietly,
we prepared to make good what
we said. The keen encounter came and
the word knows. The result is easy and
pleasant for those folks of the present
generation to talk and write the days of
yore, but they little know, neither can
they imagine the suffering of those fear-
ful days. And there is one thing I much
fear; and that is, that the American peo-
ple do not appreciate the boon of free-
dom. Party spirit is becoming stronger,
and unless it is checked, will tumble into
ruin the noble spirit of the Republic.
But let me hasten to my narrative.

From the opening of the revolution we
experienced all phases of fortune—now
good and now ill, at one time victorious,
at another, conquered. The darkest per-
iod we had, however, was, I think, when
Washington after several reverses, re-
treated to the Valley Forge; where he
resolved to pass the winter of it. All
have often seen the tears coursing down
our Commander's careworn cheeks as he
would be conversing with the continental
officer about the condition of his sol-
diers. You have doubtless heard the
story of Washington going into a thick
et to pray. Well, it is not true; he used
often to pray in secret for aid and com-
fort from God, the interposition of whose
divine providence brought us safely
through those dark days of tradition.

I can remember it well—the
chilly wind whistled and howled through
the leafless trees, though the sky was
cloudless and the sun shining brightly;
he remained in his quarters nearly the
whole of the afternoon alone. When he
came out I noticed his face was a bit
paler than usual, and that there seemed
to be something in his mind of more than
ordinary importance. Returning in, he
before dusk he dispatched an orderly to

preliminary conversation, which lasted

cal Culture, Articulation, Enuncia-

singing. All books will be furnished
free and will consist of the chor-

course. An effort will be made to
entertain persons from a distance
too, but we are not able to say

ise that. The week will end with a
grand Concert, made up of selections

it promises to be the best opportunity

great music instructions. We,

musical people, to this fine opening,
that they may all be able to notify their
friends and enjoy a musical feast
together.

Transit of vegetable food on the canals fell off from

SUMNER'S SPEECH,

The long expected speech of Mr. Sumner comes to us in full to-day. It is one of his most studied and exhaustive efforts and, we regret to say, shows no improvement in temper towards the President. Indeed, it seems rather like an attempt to arraign the Administration and its supporters, than candid discussion of the main question of annexing San Domingo. Mr. Sumner's main effort is to prove that the preliminaries of negotiation have been attended by threatening demonstrations towards Hayti.

He alleges that International law has been violated by belligerent intervention "maintaining usurper in power that he might sell his country." This, he claims, has been done without warrant of the law or constitution. This he tries to prove by a vast display of historical learning, searching the past diplomacy of Spain, to put it in unfavorable contrast with our own. To Spain, he credits delicate regard for the rights of San Domingo and magnanimous forbearance. Upon us he charges rapacity and unprincipled greed of territory.

This parallel is a weak one, and will not resist the assaults of truth. His charges are baseless when the facts are known. Mr. Sumner's argument reads very much like the standing Democratic complaint that General Grant controls elections at the South with the bayonet, when the fact is, there are not soldiers enough in the United States to control the elections even in little Rhode Island.

Whatever may be said of the merits of the speech, we think all will agree, that it was in bad taste, as to time. The San Domingo commissioners have just arrived, and it would have been simply fair and respectful, to hear their report, before opening the discussion upon its merits. As the President refers the whole matter to the action of Congress, this vindictive attack upon him might well have been spared, and it is certainly effectively parried, by his own discreet and sagacious policy.

In reply to Mr. Sumner, Mr. Howe (Rep., Wis.) cited various historical instances in which public men, who had been regarded with universal esteem by their countrymen, had, by subsequent acts of misguided zeal and passion, forfeited that confidence and relapsed into obscurity, or assumed positions at utter variance with their former declarations. In this connection, he referred to the prominence and influence of ex-Secretary Seward, Chief Justice Chase and Mr. Sumner in 1861. The last seen of the first of this great triumvirate, he had turned his back upon the hopes, lessons, and friends of his better years, and was acting as a master of ceremonies in a political pageant wherein an itinerant President was the principal figure. The second had employed the authority of the great office of the Chief Justice of the United States to undo and annul the most beneficent act of his civil administration. To-day the Republican party experienced some of that anguish which swelled the breast of Caesar, when, having already been struck by Casca and Cassius, he saw a third dagger uplifted by the hand of a dear friend, and there was wrung from his agonized bosom the exclamation "Et tu Brute." For, to-day, we had heard the remaining member of that great triumvirate, that Senator, who had so earnestly urged upon reluctant Senators the purchase of those rigid, far-off regions of the North Pole, now turning a deaf ear to the echoes which brought back his own exultant prophecy that our city could be nothing less than the whole American continent, with her gates upon all the surrounding seas. To-day the Senator arose not only to oppose the annexation of an Island at our very doors, but to denounce as criminal a President who had ventured to the exercise of a strictly constitutional prerogative, to advise its acquisition. Mr. Howe had sought the privilege of entering an appearance here for that illustrious respondent. He would file no demurrer nor interpose any dilatory pleas, but preferred the general issue.

country, and above all, an energetic and indus-
trious population. He was pleased with the or-
ganization of these old settlers meetings. This
was the first he had attended, but he hoped to
have the pleasure of being at them for years to
come.

Mr. J. S. Armstrong made few remarks. He
recollected the time when the surveyors in 1851
were surveying the canal, and wondered whether he should ever see, at the mouth of the Fox
river, town as large as Newark, Ohio, where
he came from. Now Ottawa was as big as half
a dozen of it. He remembered the time when
Chicago was not as big as Ottawa is now. At one
time he knew every farmer between this and
Peoria. When they met on the prairie, they did
not merely nod and pass on, as they do now, but
stopped and talked and inquired about each
other.

Mr. Taylor, of Massachusetts, related some
reminiscences of the early settlement of Massa-
chusetts notwithstanding pathetic appeal from
Brother Batcheller to "be short."

Mr. Perry A. Armstrong said he knew most of
the people assembled around him for about for-
ty years. He remembered when their nearest
neighbors were four miles off, when railroads
were unknown and unheard of, when the first
stern wheel boat that came up the Illinois river
was thing of wonder and when, if they wanted
to go to Chicago, they must either go on
horseback or by the stage at the rate of six cents
a mile. It was thought great improvement
when the packets on the canal took them from
Ottawa in the afternoon, and they could wake
up in Chicago in the morning. At that time,
farmers were generally afraid of the prairie, and
preferred to settle in the vicinity of timber land,
but now, everybody knows that the best farms
are on the prairie land and away from the tim-
ber.

Deacon Gum, of La Salle, was called upon
but declined to make any remarks as he was so
full of "reminiscences of the Black Hawk war that
if he began he would not be able to close until
after the hour fixed for adjournment.

Rev. Mr. Batcheller then said there was no
old settler present whose children and grandchildren
now living numbered so. The great pros-
perity of this State was owing to the moral
and intellectual character of its citizens, and if
there was any country worth having, it must
be a moral country. He thanked the meeting
for the attention they had given to all the
speakers.

Mr. A. N. Ebersol, Secretary of the Society,
reported that during the past year the following
members had died:

Sylvanus Crook, of South Ottawa, settled in
the county in 1855, died in July, 1871 age 85.

ing of his head. As we approached near him, we discovered
that he was an old acquaintance,
but that in his besotted condition
of drunkenness—and it was not yet
ten o'clock in the morning—he did
not recognize us at all. We were
deeply pained at the spectacle.
Upon nearer inspection we observed
that he was without a shirt. He
staggered along the street and down
Dearborn, to a place where rum
was sold, went in, and taking a
chair, soon became lost to his sur-
roundings in a stolid condition of
complete intoxication. We have
not seen more complete wreck in
many years, and doubt whether
there is in the whole city of Chica-
go, a single man, who seen on the
street, would be taken as a more
thorough representative of drunk-
enness—or the gutter—than this
poor, shirtless, abject man.


Ten years ago we knew that man
a popular and prominent member
of the Legislature of one of our
great Northwestern States. Soon
after we met him in the great Chi-
cago Wigwam of 1869, member
of the convention which first nomi-
nated Lincoln for the Presidency.
Again we met him in Washington,
where he had much influence with
the delegates from his State. He
went into the staff department of
the army sometime during the war,
and immediately after its close made
some fortunate speculations by
which he became a rich man. But
about two years ago he entered into speculations which turned out
badly, and he was swamped in busi-
ness. A few months after that we
met him at the Briggs House one
evening and thought he was slightly
under the influence of liquor; we
had no idea that he had begun to
move down that inclined plane
which has brought him to the gut-
ter and a life of unutterable misery.
He is the husband of an intelligent
and highly cultivated lady, and the
father of children who, few years
ago, were as happy as any now liv-
ing on Wabash Avenue. Whether
these have been dragged down to
the father's degradation we do not
know. Oh, thou invisible spirit of
wine, if thou hast no other name to
be called by, let us call you the
DEVIL. Chicago Evening Post.

Paris, 29. Sept. - Die letzten Abende sind mit großer Aufregung wegen des Schicksals des Komitees und der anderen Leiter der Commune vergangen. Court for this county. The suit was to recover
a note for eleven thousand dollars and interest
given for horse sold by Mr. Lyford to Mr. Cut-
ter. The referees award to Mr. Lyford eleven
thousand eight hundred and thirty-four dol-
lars and sixteen cents. The costs of the refer-
ence, 1870, also falling to the defendant to pay.
One of our city clergymen exchanged pulpits
Sabbath or two since with a brother clergy-
man of Lewiston. It so happened that the pul-
pit was too low for his near sighted optics, and
he was under the necessity of piling up Bible
and hymn books whereon to place his manu-
script. He began his sermon and was declaim-
ing it with wonderful enthusiasm, when by a
unlucky gesture he struck the cover of the BIBLE,
up it flew and tipped the sermon to the
floor. Hymn books, bible, stationery, fell with
a loud noise to the floor. To add to the misfor-
tune, the sheets of the sermon were loose and
were scattered hither and thither, like autumn
leaves, over the church. The crisis for the
minister—how to get out of it, with utmost
goodness and self-possession, the minister, taking a bird's eye glance at the wreck of his at-
fairs on the floor below, turned to the congre-
gation and said, "I trust my friends, this may
be an emblem that the good seed may be sown
as these sheets have been sown," and without
troubling the disheveled manuscript further,
took up the thread of his discourse and extern-
porized the latter half of the sermon with gen-
eral approbation.

ARROOSTOOK COUNTY.

The Pioneer says last season Mr. Howe of
Monticello dug a well near his barn, and left it
unstoned, covering it with rails. Last Thurs-
day, as he was driving near the spot with a
pair of horses attached to a sled, one of them
broke through the covering to the well, drag-
ging the other after it. When extricated they
were both dead.

PENOBSCOT COUNTY.

The Bangor Whig states that John McClure
of that city was arrested Thursday on war-
rant charging him with the murder of his wife
who died suddenly some months since.
The Bath Times says some time in the early
part of next week Waterville will be reached by
rail.

SAGADAHOC COUNTY.

The Bath Times says last Friday evening in
Bowdoinham, as two boys were coasting down
Back street, their sled ran into a passing team
with such force as to prostate the horse, and
one of the boys named Curtis fractured his leg
and received other bad head wounds, whilst
the other boy on the sled was also severely in-
jured. At last accounts both boys were rapidly
improving.

The Times says very small amount of ice
will be put in store at Richmond this winter.

SOMERSET COUNTY.

A town meeting was held in Arbor last Sat-
urday to see if the town would release the con-
dition annexed to the town subscription to the
capital stock of the Somerset Railroad Co., so
that if the stockholders shall deem it suitable
and proper, the company may issue bonds to
complete the road and secure the same by
mortgage of said road and franchises with-
out coming to direct vote upon the question.
The town by vote of 95 to 2 adjourned to the
28th of January, and further voted that the di-
rectors of the Somerset railroad be requested to
confer with the directors of the Consolidated
Maine Central Railroad Co, to see on what
terms, if any, they will lease or otherwise aid
in the completion of the Somerset road and re-
port the result of such conference at such ad-
journed meeting.

WALDO COUNTY.

Miss Arethusa Vose, of Belfast, aged about
55 years, was found dead in her bed last Mon-
day morning. She was well as usual the day
before, and probably died of heart disease.

YORK COUNTY.

The carriage shop of Mr. Kimball on Waite
street, Saco, was destroyed by fire on Tuesda-
y night about 11 o'clock.

TREATIES AND PROCLAMATIONS.
A PROCLAMATION by the President of the United States and Great Britain respecting Claims, fisheries, navigation of the St. Lawrence, ETC., American lumber on the river St. John, Boundary-concluded, May 8, 1871; notifications exchanged June 11, 1871; proclaimed July 4, 1871.

Whereas, treaty between the United States of America and Her Britannic Majesty, Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, concerning the settlement of disputes between the two countries, was concluded and signed at Washington by the high commissioners and plenipotentiaries of the respective governments on the eight day of May last; which treaty is, word for word, as follows:

The United States of America and Her Britannic Majesty, being desirous to provide for an amicable settlement of all disputes, have for that purpose appointed their respective plenipotentiaries, that is to say: the President of the United States has appointed, on the part of the United States, as commissioners in a joint high commission and plenipotentiaries, Hamilton Fish, Secretary of State; Robert Cumming Schomburgk, envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary to Great Britain; Samuel Nelson, an Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States; Ebenezer Rockwood Hoar, of Massachusetts; and George Henry Williams, of Oregon; and Her Britannic Majesty, on her part, has appointed as her high commissioners and plenipotentiaries, the Right Honorable George Frederick Samuel, Earl De Grey and Earl of Ripon, Viscount Goderich, Baron Lyveden of the United Kingdom, Lord President of Her Majesty's Most Honorable Privy Council, Knight of the Most Noble Order of the Garter, etc., etc.; the Right Honorable Sir Stafford Henry Northcote, Baronet, one of Her Majesty's Most Honorable Privy Council, member of Parliament, Companion of the Most Honorable Order of the Bath, etc., etc.; Sir Edward Thornton, knight, Commander of the Most Honorable Order of the Bath, Her Majesty's envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary to the United States of America; Sir John Alexander Macdonald, Knight Commander of the Most Honorable Order of the Bath, member of Her Majesty's Privy Council for Canada, and Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Her Majesty's Dominion of Canada; and Montague Bernard, Esquire, Chichele Professor of international law in the University of Oxford.

And the said plenipotentiaries, after having exchanged their full powers, which were found to be in due and proper form, have agreed to and concluded the following articles:

ARTICLE I.

WHEREAS, Differences have arisen between the government of the United States and the government of Her Britannic Majesty, and still exist, growing out of the acts committed by the several vessels which have given rise to the claims generically known as the Alabama claims;

And whereas, Her Britannic Majesty has authorized her high commissioners to express, in a friendly spirit, the regret felt by Her Majesty's government for the escape, under whatever circumstances, of the Alabama and other vessels from British ports, and for the depredations committed by those vessels;

Now, in order to remove and adjust all complaints and claims on the part of the United States, and to provide for the speedy settlement of such claims, which are not disputed by Her Britannic Majesty's government, the high contracting parties agree that all the said claims, growing out of acts by the aforesaid vessels and known as the "Alabama claims," shall be referred to a tribunal of arbitration to be composed of five arbitrators, to be appointed in the following manner, that is to say: One shall be named by the President of the United States; one shall be named by Her Britannic Majesty; His Majesty the King of Italy shall be requested to name one; the President of the Swiss Confederation shall be requested to name one; and His Majesty the Emperor of Brazil shall be requested to name one.

In case of the death, absence, or incapacity to serve of any or either of the said arbitrators, or, in the event of either of the said arbitrators emitting or declining or ceasing to act as such, the President of the United States, or Her Britannic Majesty, or His Majesty the King of Italy, or the President of the Swiss Confederation, or His Majesty the Emperor of Brazil, as the case may be, may forthwith name another person to act as arbitrator in the place and stead of the arbitrator originally named by each head of a State.

And in the event of the refusal or omission for two months after receipt of the request from either of the high contracting parties of His Majesty the King of Italy or the President of the Swiss Confederation, or His Majesty the Emperor of Brazil, to name an arbitrator either to fulfill the original appointment or in the place of one who may have died, be absent, or incapacitated, or to name, decline, or from any cause cease to act as such arbitrator, His Majesty the King of Sweden and Norway shall be requested to name one or more persons, as the case may be, to act as such arbitrators.

ARTICLE II.

The arbitrators shall meet at Geneva, at the earliest convenient day after they shall have been named, and shall proceed impartially and carefully to examine and decide all questions that shall be laid before them on the part of the governments of the United States and Her Britannic Majesty, respectively. All questions considered by the tribunal, including the final award, shall be decided by a majority of all the arbitrators. Each of the high contracting parties shall carefully name one person to attend the tribunal as its agent to represent it generally in all matters connected with the arbitration.

ARTICLE III.

The written or printed case of each of the parties, accompanied by the documents, official correspondence, and other evidence on which each relies, shall be delivered in duplicate to each of the arbitrators and to the agent of the other party as soon as may be after the organization of the tribunal, but within a period not exceeding three months from the date of the exchange of the publications of this treaty.

ARTICLE IV.

Within four months after the delivery of the written or printed case, each party may, in like manner, deliver at duplicate to each of said arbitrators and to the agent of the other party, a counter case and additional documents, correspondence and evidence in reply to the documents, correspondence and evidence so presented by the other party. The arbitrators may, however, extend the time for delivering such counter case, documents, correspondence and evidence.

Kendall, the gardener, on Sunday morning last, was not able to do more than simply announce the fact.

It appears that Mr. Kendall has been in the habit of turning his horses and mules into an out-lot where he allowed them to remain until near midnight, when he would stable them; but, on Saturday night, he fell into sound slumber and allowed the usual hour for stabling to pass unnoticed. Between one and two o'clock in the morning, Mrs. Kendall arose, saw her husband and reminded him that the stock had not been put under cover. Mr. Kendall immediately repaired to the out-lot, and missing the stock, went out upon the road to look for them. He soon encountered three men, one leading the mare, saddled, and the other two leading three mules. He instantly snatched the bridle of the mare, and leading her pursued the thieves who had the mules in charge. Steadily gaining upon them, and coming near, he ordered them to let go the stock. At this moment one of the thieves discharged the contents of a shotgun at the pursuer, and wounded him in the breast and right arm. The thieves then released the mules and fled.

Neighbors of Mr. Kendall, who had heard the report of the gun, came in, and ascertaining the fact, came to the city and reported to Chief Myers, who, with Sergeant Irwin, immediately went in pursuit.

The officers soon came to the conclusion that the thieves had intended to steal the horses and swim them to the Missouri shore. They tracked the rogues to the Mississippi levee near Kline's brick yard, where they lost the scent. The officers then passed down the levee to the point, where they ascertained that two men had been seen rowing a skiff up the Ohio and over to the Kentucky shore. These men the officers concluded were two of the thieves. Pursuing the clue further, the officers learned that Jock Owens had been seen on Saturday evening rowing a skiff down the river toward the point; that he and his brother and Harris had been in the habit of harboring in a flat boat moored against the Kentucky shore; that they had been seen together late on Saturday night; that one of the saddles stolen by the thieves belonged to Morgan, of the Eames' Hub and Spoke factory, and that Harris had been his driver and knew where the saddle was kept; that the 9th, saddle it was said, belonged to Easley; and that Jock had been at Easley's house as late as 11 o'clock Saturday night; that one of the thieves—the one who shot—was a tall man with an extraordinarily large foot, and that Dick Owens had feet to fill this part of the bill. Acting upon this information, and other facts not proper to be mentioned at this time, Jock and Dick Owens and Jessy Harris were arrested on Sunday morning.

the forest accessible to the furnace men of the Hoosatonic and Harlem valleys. Already, they have made large purchases at half a dozen different points, erected perpetual charcoal kilns, and are beginning to ship large quantities of charcoal. This source of supply will allow and encourage a large increase of furnaces, and the supply of iron ore and charcoal may now be considered inexhaustible.

Whether he belonged to "the Church" or not.

Next down to the river Quaker strayed;
His dress of a sober hue was made.
"My coat and my hat must be all of gray,
And wear them must on my Heavenward way."
So he buttoned his coat straight up to his chin,
And staidly, solemnly waded in,
And his broad-brimmed beaver he pulled down tight
For a head cold and white.
But a strong wind carried away his hat,
And a moment he wistfully gazed at that;
And then, as he looked to the further shore,
His coat slipped off and was seen no more.
As he entered Heaven his suit of gray
Went quietly sailing away, away;
And none of the angels questioned him
About the width of his beaver's brim;
There, the only dress for which angels care.

A Scotsman, next, with King David's Psalms,
Clasping them tight in his aged arms,
Believing 'twould be an unheard-of thing
If the ransomed in Heaven aught else should sing.
But heard him heave an anxious sigh
As he saw the river run broad and high;
And astonished he looked, as like a stone,
The book of his "Psalms" in the waves went down;
And he found that in Heaven the countless throngs
Sing only, and ever, the Lamb's He-song.

Next came, with serious, solemn look,
A Wesleyan with his Methodist "Book."
In the fullness of faith through the waves he pressed,
Looking upward, with joy, to his coming rest;
But he saw, as he turned his glance below,
That the water had soaked his Discipline through;
And that next, on the river, far and wide,
It floated away on the rolling tide,
While the saint, astonished, passed through alone,
Without his "Discipline" up to the throne,
Forever assured, in that blessed place,
That he never again should fall from grace.

Two saints came next to the river's brink,
But one from the other appeared to shrink;
And as they were passing along the way,
Heard the one to the other say:
"I fear, indeed, that you've not, my friend,
Rightly attained unto life's great end;
You've had but few drops on your brow,
While I have been plunged, as you'll see me now,
And really think it will hardly do,
As I'm 'close-communion,' to cross with you;
You're going, grant, to the world of bliss,
But do so that way, and I'll do this."
So straightway plunging with all his might,
Away to the left, and his friend to the right,
Apart they went from this world of sin,
But saw that together they entered in,
The light of eternity making it plain,
That plunging or sprinkling, alike, is vain;
That the water itself was meant to be
The emblem of inward purity;
That the mode is nothing—the only flood
That can cleanse from sin is the Saviour's blood.

And, now, where the river was rolling high,
A Presbyterian Church drew nigh,
The Bible each right hand firmly grasped,
While "Confessions of Faith" in the left they clasped;
Their leaders were marked with thought profound,

A GANG BROKEN UP IN OHIO


CLEVELAND, June 27.—In April last United States Marshal Hastings, of the Northern District of Ohio ascertained that a considerable amount of counterfeit greenbacks, National bank notes and fractional currency was circulating in Northern Ohio and Eastern Indiana and that a large gang of operators were engaged in their manufacture. Two of the most skillful detectives in the Secret Service Department were detailed to assist Marshal Hastings in the matter and in the past months they have succeeded in breaking up the gang. Arrests have been made in time and several of the ringleaders, some of the most notable, termed Isaac Monroe Bisse of Alliance, Wm. H. Barr of Van Wert, John Hickman, Christopher Brady and Geo. A. Shawen of Marion, Geo. Frederick of Decatur, Ind., Matthew A. Boyd of New Cumberland, Ohio, Harry Porter, Joe Warren and other well-known rascals, have been arrested and a great deal of counterfeit money seized. Shawen turned state's evidence and was one of those Government detectives who were working at Fort Wayne, and who had succeeded in ingratiating themselves into the confidence of the counterfeiters.


ARRESTS IN GEORGIA—ATTEMPTED RESCUE OF THE PRISONERS—A LEGISLATOR IMPLICATED.


From The Augusta Chronicle, June 27.—The officers of the Secret Service Division of the Treasury Department, who went south about a month since on important business, returned here Saturday. They arrested Romulus Noble and Elias Sweat, at Fernandina, Fla., and O. J. Sexton, an engraver, at [place] for counterfeit five dollar gold and 5 cent and 10 cent silver coin of the United States. A few days subsequent Tebeauville was charged with the same offense; he had perfected extensive highly intended for circulation in the West India Islands and the nine principals of an organized gang in the vicinity of Fernandina by frequent and wanton violations of the law. A large quantity of counterfeit gold and silver coin admirably found their way when arrested and there were secured at the same time, ready for shipment per steamer to Sackett's Harbor, several cases containing heavy machinery, German silver ingots of composition metal, English alloy copper used principally in the manufacture of the cent, gold and gold dust, galvanic battery complete, crucibles, engraving tools and other articles in the very best condition. The three named prisoners were taken before the United States Commissioner, where they committed to jail; Noble in default $4,000 and the others $500 each. Shortly in the evening, a mob of men, about 50 in number, masked and otherwise disguised, assembled for the purpose of rescuing the prisoners. Their attention was drawn to the fact that service men had arrested Noble and his companions and would arrive by train just then. The mob proceeded to the depot, boarded the train through each and searching every nook with lanterns and when necessary, alarming those who were asleep. At the time Government officials arrived in the town by another conveyance, took the prisoners from the train and safely embarked with them on board the United States revenue cutter, the commander of which, in compliance with special requests, conveyed the PRISONERS to Port Jefferson, Dry. The following day, however, a leading merchant of the city furnished requisite bail, and a large sum was also advanced by his friends to be used in securing legal counsel. On last Saturday, Secret Service officers in the course of their investigations arrested in Blakely, Ga., Capt. Daniel F. Knowles, representing a member of the Legislature from Pierce county, and arrested Thomas Sweat, taking them to Savannah. Knowles is charged with complicity in the gold counterfeit operations of the Noble, Sweat and Sexton gang and is charged with conduct regarded as forfeiture of bond or such violation of law as to make him liable, he having taken into his hands, nine pieces of gold, noting the harm which would accrue therefrom. It appears that he bought stock of gold in Atlanta for $500, which represented as gold being in fact the counterfeit gold coin and to-day the bogus took its way back to another person in Lake City, Florida, from whom he had originally bought it.

The Dock Commissioners have advertised
for proposals for large quantities of materials
for the construction of the proposed new piers
and bulkheads. The latter are to be of
massive granite, and the piers will be composed, some of wood and others of iron or
stone. The avenue along the water front
will be widened to about two hundred feet,
and will completely environ the city, giving
ample space for the movement of freight and
the transaction of all river business, while it
will also be the route of belt railroad.
These improvements are of the very highest
importance to the city. Our present docks
and piers are not only unpleasant to the sight
and smell, and calculated to impress stran-
gers coming here for the first time with an
exaggerated contempt for the metropolis itself,
but they are obstructions in the way of busi-
ness and are generally dangerous to indi-
vidual safety, not only from their rickety con-
dition, but from the dangerous classes of city
Arabs that infest them at night. Our river
fronts, with their immense wealth piled at all
times upon them, should be kept as brilliantly
lighted at night as Broadway, and the places
of ill repute that have made Water street
and other thoroughfares in the vicinity of the
rivers public disgrace should be rooted out.
The pier improvements contemplated by the
Dock Commissioners will secure all these
improvements. The business community will soon move away the
sailors' dens and dance houses of Water
street, and the broad Riverside avenue, when
completed, will be found as inviting to the
honest denizens of the Fourth and Sixth and
other lowly wards of the city, as the Battery,
under the new identifying influence of the
Park Commissioners, has already become to
our First warders. In fact, the remodelling
of the piers and river fronts will prove to be
letting of light into the dark passages of
Baxter, Roosevelt, West and other streets
similarly situated—a sort of Haussmannic
cleansing of our Faubourg St. Antoine.


While our Commissioners are showing highly
commendable zeal in their prosecution of
this work, they must remember that the opening of Hell Gate is possible next year, and
that great developments may to some extent
upset their plans. There is no doubt that the
shortening of the route from Europe will trans-
fer great portion of the shipping to the upper
part of the island and compel sudden indus-
try in the matter of pier building about Har-
lem, while the necessity for a complete pier
system on the southern portions of the island
may no longer be so absolute. We do not hold
that Fifth avenue will be transferred to the
Battery because of the Hell Gate opening, nor
that Central Park will have to be built up with
warehouses, as some croaking philosophers
suggest, because our Southern coast trade will
always line our southern river fronts, and as
many of our great European steamers already
have their docks in Jersey City, their removal
to Harlem would not be likely to create dis-
astrous revolution, except for Jersey; but
there can be no question that granite docks
will soon be required in the neighborhood of
Harlem. While the coast is comparatively
clear, therefore, we would advise our Com-
missioners to commence building there.

It would be a certain gain, Aaron,
if it saved you from bankruptcy, with
which, as I understand it, you are
threatened.'


I think, said Aaron, we could
get on without that. I like the idea
of your coming into my warehouse
and taking Hobson's place. All the
money from retail sales passes through
his hands, and he has it in his power,
if not honest, to rob me seriously. I've
not felt altogether easy in regard to
him of late. Why, I can hardly tell.
I've seen nothing wrong. But if you
take his place, twelve hundred dollars
will be saved certainly.'


'But if I have my house to keep,'
Mrs. Little answered to this, 'how
can I help you at the warehouse? The
first thing in order is to get the house
off my hands.'


'Don't you think that Annie could
be induced to come and live with us
for a few months, until we try the new
experiment?'


'But the money, Aaron; the mon-
ey this furniture would bring? That
is what I'm looking after. You want
money now.'


'Very true.
Then let us hang out the flag.'


'I know that mother will not
let Annie leave home, so it is no use to
think of it. The flag, Aaron, the red
flag! Depend upon it, that's the right
thing to be done. Fifteen or sixteen
hundred dollars in hand will make you
feel like another person, give you
courage, confidence and energy.'
'You may be right, Betsy, but
I cannot bear the thought of running
out the flag of which you talk so
lightly.'


'Shall I say coward? Are you afraid
to do what common prudence tells you
is right?'


'I was afraid, Betsy, but am no
longer faint-hearted. With such a
brave little wife as you to stand by my
side, I need not fear the world.'


One week from that day, the red
flag was hung out. When the auc-
tioneer made up his accounts, he had
in hand a little over three thousand
dollars, for which a check was filled
out to the order of Aaron Little. It
came into his hands just at the right
moment, and made him feel, to use
his own words, 'as easy as an old
shoe.' One week later, Mrs. Little
took the place of Mr. Hobson, as chief
manager and cash receiver in her hus-
band's warehouse. There were some
few signs of rebellion among the clerk
and shop girls at the beginning; but
Mrs. Little had a quick steady eye, and
a self-reliant manner, that assisted
her presence to be felt as a master's.
In a lapse of half a year.

HONOLULU, Dec. 18th, 1870
GENTLEMEN—Referring to our conversation this
morning on the subsidy for an Australian Steamer,
I state that the Government is ready to take
into immediate consideration contracts that may be
proposed by the Agent of the Y. P. T. Company, or
of any responsible Company, whose steam service
shall carry out the conditions specified in the Ap-
propriation Bill, always bearing in mind the rela-
tions of Mr. Hall to the service which he has uni-
ted with great labor and risk to himself and whom
we desire to treat with consideration.
The wording of the subsidy item you are familiar
with, as copy of it has been sent to you from this
Department.

Speaking for myself I anticipate that speedy ar-
rangement may be effected, as the establishment
of satisfactory line seems very likely to be made
by the countries that interested in the project.

I remain, yours truly,

Signed J. N. SMITH,

Minister of Finance.
Messrs. Hackfeld & Co., Agents of P. T. Co.,
Honolulu.

BATHING in the Dead Sea produces as
novel sensation as if you found yourself
suddenly endowed with wings, and emu
lating the feats of a atumbler- pigeon in mid
air. You become a clumsy float, top
heavy buoy, a swollen cork, the instant
you are in its waters, and arms, legs, and
body are apparently endowed with the
strangest qualities. 1t is as if heavy
weights were affixed to each directly you
attempt to move. and experienced swim
mers fail in their best strokes, by reason
of the unnatural buoyancy with which
they have to contend. Your limbs are on
the surface, and you cleave the air with
yonr hands, the moment you try to swim,
and the man who would be drowned as
soon as he was out Of his depth in any
other sheet of water in the world is the
one best fitted for bathing in the Dead Sea-
He cannot sink in il, let him do what he
will 1t is as if he were incased In lie
belts, or sprawling on featherbed. Ii
he lean back and throw his feet up, it is
exactly as ifhe were resting in peculiarly
well-stuffed easy-chair, with leg rest to
match. He may fold his arms, turn on
one side, lie flat upon his stomach or back,
clasp his knees with both hands, or draw
toes and head together, in the shape the
human body would assume if crammed





out, and all with no more possibility of
sinking than if he were in so much soft
sand. Woe to him if he be tempted by
these unusual facilities to stay long in the
water with his head uncoveredl The
bare and rocky walls of the low-lying
caldron which holds the Sea of Death re-
fleet back the burning sun and oencen-
trate its rays; and coup de soseI will be
the all but inevitable consequence OF his
imprudence. Two of our party entered
the water, and remained in it some seconds
before they recovered their heads, and
the result was severe shooting pains, sick
ness, and dizziness, which lasted until
their immersion, an hour later, in the re-
freshing waters of the Jordan. Woe too,
to the inexperienced stranger, who, fol-
lowing his rule in other bathing, dips his
head as well as his body, into the Dead
Sea. Inflamed eyes and nostrils, together
with hair and beard laden with acrid
salts, are among the penalties of his rash
ness: while if he taste its waters, he be-
comes acquainted with greater concen-
tration of nastiness than had entered into
his imagination before. In buoyancy and
bitterness the Sea of Sodom exceeded all
we had heard or read respecting it; but
in some other particulars our anticipations
were falsified surprisingly. We looked
for gloom, and we found brightness; We
had imagined turbid waters, and we found
lake exquisitely clear and delicately
blue; we expected perfect silence and an
unbroken waste, and we found the birds
singing sweetly among the tamarisks and
oleanders, which spring up wherever q
stream finds its way from the mountains
to mingle with the mysterious inland sea.
